items.readable_text:
Content:
An important family of distributions in probability and statistics is the student's [MATH: t]-distribution (or [MATH: t]-distribution). The diagram below shows the probability density functions for some members of this family.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c9d3d279405caf419fc861018939dedf]

Content:
Each family member has an associated positive integer parameter [MATH: k,] known as the degrees of freedom.

Content:
The probability density function of a student's [MATH: t]-distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped, similar to the standard normal distribution. However, [MATH: t]-distribution curves have fatter "tails." A consequence is that extreme events (i.e., events far from the mean) are more likely with a [MATH: t]-distribution than a standard normal distribution.

Content:
To see how the student's [MATH: t]-distribution comes about, consider a large random sample of size [MATH: n]

Content:
[MATH: X_1, \: X_2, \: \ldots, \: X_{n}]

Content:
drawn from a population with mean [MATH: \mu] and variance [MATH: \sigma^2.] According to the central limit theorem,

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\overline{X}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \approx N(0,1),]

Content:
where [MATH: \overline{X}] is the sample mean.

Content:
In reality, it's unlikely that the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2] is known, in which case it must be estimated.

Content:
Recall that an unbiased estimator for [MATH: \sigma^2,] known as the sample variance, is given by

Content:
[MATH: S^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( X_i - \overline{X} \right)^2.]

Content:
If we estimate [MATH: \sigma^2] using [MATH: S^2,] then it can be shown that

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\overline{X}-\mu}{S/\sqrt{n}} \approx T_{n-1}]

Content:
where [MATH: T_{n-1}] is a [MATH: t]-distributed random variable with [MATH: n-1] degrees of freedom.

Content:
The [MATH: t]-distribution is widely used in statistical estimation problems. We'll learn more about the practical applications of this important distribution in future lessons.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
An important family of distributions in probability and statistics is the student's [MATH: t]-distribution (or [MATH: t]-distribution). The diagram below shows the probability density functions for some members of this family.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c9d3d279405caf419fc861018939dedf]

Content:
Each family member has an associated positive integer parameter [MATH: k,] known as the degrees of freedom.

Content:
The probability density function of a student's [MATH: t]-distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped, similar to the standard normal distribution. However, [MATH: t]-distribution curves have fatter "tails." A consequence is that extreme events (i.e., events far from the mean) are more likely with a [MATH: t]-distribution than a standard normal distribution.

Content:
To see how the student's [MATH: t]-distribution comes about, consider a large random sample of size [MATH: n]

Content:
[MATH: X_1, \: X_2, \: \ldots, \: X_{n}]

Content:
drawn from a population with mean [MATH: \mu] and variance [MATH: \sigma^2.] According to the central limit theorem,

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\overline{X}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \approx N(0,1),]

Content:
where [MATH: \overline{X}] is the sample mean.

Content:
In reality, it's unlikely that the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2] is known, in which case it must be estimated.

Content:
Recall that an unbiased estimator for [MATH: \sigma^2,] known as the sample variance, is given by

Content:
[MATH: S^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( X_i - \overline{X} \right)^2.]

Content:
If we estimate [MATH: \sigma^2] using [MATH: S^2,] then it can be shown that

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\overline{X}-\mu}{S/\sqrt{n}} \approx T_{n-1}]

Content:
where [MATH: T_{n-1}] is a [MATH: t]-distributed random variable with [MATH: n-1] degrees of freedom.

Content:
The [MATH: t]-distribution is widely used in statistical estimation problems. We'll learn more about the practical applications of this important distribution in future lessons.

---

Item 12 — Tutorial: Comparing the T-Distribution With the Normal Distribution

The shape of the student's [MATH: t]-distribution is similar to that of the standard normal distribution. Are they related, and if so, how?

Content:
The two distributions are indeed related. In fact, we have the following theorem:

Content:
> The student's [MATH: t]-distribution [MATH: T_k] approaches [MATH: N(0,1)] as [MATH: k \to \infty.]
